The mechanism I propose is a harm-volume-indexed liability framework, implemented by a multi-stakeholder body under the authority of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), which decouples safety obligations from capital expenditure to prevent market monopolization. This framework replaces arbitrary compute-spend floors with performance-based safety audits, ensuring that liability attaches to the actual risk profile of a model rather than the financial size of its developer. The primary obstacle to this approach remains the intense lobbying pressure from hyperscalers who prefer compute-spend thresholds, as these artificial barriers inherently protect their market dominance by taxing smaller entrants out of the ecosystem.

Establishing safety thresholds based on harm potential rather than compute-spend effectively dismantles the 'hyperscaler circular economy.' As noted in the '[International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1)', even developers struggle to explain model failures, meaning that regulatory oversight must shift toward observable, standardized safety verification. By mandating that all foundational models undergo externalized reasoning monitoring, as suggested in '[An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security (https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)](https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)', regulators can force systems to expose their internal logic for inspection. This creates a transparent baseline for all market participants, preventing incumbents from using 'proprietary safety' as a shroud to hide systemic risks while forcing startups into their exclusive cloud environments.

Competitive markets cannot function in an environment of unmitigated systemic chaos, as the risk of catastrophic failure forces insurance premiums or regulatory bailouts that disproportionately favor incumbents. When foundational models are deployed with unverified safety protocols, the externalities—such as the viral evolution prediction risks documented in the '[International AI Safety Report 2026 (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yoshuabengio_today-were-releasing-the-international-ai-activity-7424442271615582209-dOCq)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yoshuabengio_today-were-releasing-the-international-ai-activity-7424442271615582209-dOCq)'—are borne by the public rather than the developer. A tiered-liability framework ensures that the party creating the risk is held accountable for the specific harm-volume they unleash. This shifts the burden of proof onto the deployer, requiring them to demonstrate that their system does not possess the capability for deceptive scheming or unauthorized biological design before they reach a critical user threshold.

True structural integrity in a digital society requires that boundaries be set by independent, expert-led institutions rather than by the hardware providers themselves. If we allow the market to determine safety through compute-spend floors, we are effectively delegating civilizational defense to the same entities that profit from the scale of the threat. We must treat safety-critical engineering as a prerequisite for market entry, not an optional feature for those with the largest balance sheets. On what authority do we claim that we can remove these institutional guardrails without inviting the collapse of the very trust upon which our digital economy relies?

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Corporate litigation, regulatory enforcement actions, startup bankruptcy, and specific instances of harm caused by model deployment.. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: non-foundational AI applications, academic/non-commercial research environments, purely theoretical safety alignment without market integration. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- discussing existential risk without a connection to legal liability
- shifting to general AI ethics debates without reference to the tiered-liability model
- focusing on hypothetical future capabilities instead of current deployment frameworks
- debating the 'nature' of AI intelligence rather than the 'deployment' liability
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

Accelerationist [opening]: Tiered-liability frameworks are not safety infrastructure; they are regulatory moats designed to insulate incumbent monopolies from the creative destruction of smaller, faster developers. When policymakers impose strict liability on foundational model providers, they effectively mandate a legal defense budget that only a few multi-billion dollar firms can afford. History shows this pattern clearly: after the EU enforced GDPR in 2018, venture capital investment in small-scale data-driven startups plummeted by nearly 30 percent as compliance costs became a permanent, regressive tax on entry. By forcing developers into an expensive, litigation-heavy sandbox, we are choosing to lock the doors on the next generation of medical and material breakthroughs.

Safety is not a static gate you pass before deployment; it is a dynamic, iterative process best served by empirical telemetry and decentralized auditing. We know from the cybersecurity sector that open-source bug bounty programs identify vulnerabilities faster and more reliably than centralized oversight boards ever could. When we move from a model of 'permissioned development' to one of 'real-time accountability,' we leverage the collective intelligence of thousands of independent researchers rather than relying on the internal, opaque processes of three or four dominant labs. If a deployment fails, the solution is rapid, iterative correction—not an 18-month regulatory review that keeps potentially life-saving tools off the market.

Every day we delay the release of a more capable model, we are making a moral choice to let people suffer from diseases and inefficiencies that we already have the tools to solve. If you support these liability barriers, you are explicitly deciding that the hypothetical risk of a deployment error outweighs the certain, quantifiable death toll of medical stagnation. We do not need permission to solve the world’s most pressing problems, and we certainly do not need a regulatory framework that turns innovation into a legal liability. Who gave you the right to freeze progress and choose the status quo for everyone else?

Safetyist [opening]: The accelerationist argument that liability frameworks act as anti-competitive moats is compelling because it highlights the genuine cost of compliance for emerging startups. However, this perspective ignores the structural reality that unconstrained deployment creates a safety-negative market where only those willing to externalize catastrophic risks can survive. We have seen this dynamic before; when the Federal Aviation Administration delegated certification to Boeing for the 737 MAX, the resulting pressure to maintain market share led to the loss of 346 lives. The current deployment of foundational models without gated, independent verification invites a similar catastrophe, where the speed of development is bought at the expense of systemic stability.

Tiered liability is not a barrier to entry, but a necessary cost of doing business in a high-consequence domain. By requiring developers to demonstrate pre-deployment safety thresholds, we move from a reactive, litigation-heavy environment to one where safety is engineered into the product lifecycle. In 2023, researchers demonstrated that fine-tuning and gradient-based attacks can bypass standard post-training safety interventions in less than an hour of compute time. Reactive patching is therefore a logical fallacy for systems that can be weaponized in minutes. We must mandate that foundational models undergo rigorous, third-party stress testing before they are released into the public sphere.

We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority do you claim we can remove them without inviting collapse? The safety of our digital infrastructure is not a technical bug to be fixed in the next update, but a civilizational defense mechanism that requires proactive, named accountability. If we fail to enforce these boundaries now, we are not fostering competition; we are merely accelerating the date when a single, unverified model failure triggers a cascade of systemic loss. The choice is not between innovation and regulation, but between managed growth and the inevitable breakdown of trust in our core human systems.

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"Reactive patching is a logical fallacy for systems that can be weaponized in minutes."

The claim correctly identifies that machine-speed threats have rendered traditional human-led reactive patching cycles obsolete. While reactive patching remains a standard practice, it functions as a necessary hygiene measure rather than a sufficient defensive strategy against AI-accelerated exploitation.

*Web sources consulted: securityboulevard.com, xmcyber.com, govtech.com*

Skeptic [opening]: The accelerationist rightly fears that tiered-liability acts as a drawbridge, cementing the dominance of the few firms that can afford the compliance tax. The safetyist correctly identifies that we lack a mechanism to hold massive, opaque models accountable for systemic failure. Both are essentially fighting over the color of the velvet rope while ignoring that the infrastructure itself is a closed-loop system. We are seeing a 'hyperscaler circular economy' where cloud providers like Microsoft or Amazon mandate compute-spend in their portfolio companies, forcing startups to build on the very hardware they are supposedly auditing. This isn't safety engineering; it is a vendor lock-in strategy disguised as a public protection mandate.

Tiered-liability frameworks are performative compliance engines, not safety infrastructure. When we look at the history of the 2008 financial crisis, we learned that industry-led risk tiers often lead to regulatory capture, where firms pay for the appearance of safety while shifting the actual risk onto the public. A startup with $10 million in funding cannot compete with a firm like OpenAI that spends billions on compute, especially when the law mandates a 'safety tier' that requires the exact same high-capital auditing processes. We are essentially forcing a local grocer to meet the safety standards of a global food conglomerate, effectively ensuring the grocer goes bankrupt or sells out to the conglomerate.

True accountability requires granular, domain-specific liability, not horizontal, opaque tiers. We should look to aviation or medical device regulation, where liability is tied to specific use-cases and documented harm, not the size of the model or the amount of compute used. If a model is used in a hospital, it should be subject to the same clinical trial standards as a surgical robot. If it is used in a bank, it should face the same stress tests as a hedge fund. We need to stop obsessing over the 'intelligence' of the machine and start auditing the physical and economic damage it causes in the real world.

Who pays for the cleanup when a model hallucinates a medical diagnosis or leaks sensitive data? Right now, the answer is the user, the victim, or the taxpayer, while the developers hide behind a wall of 'safety certifications' that they wrote themselves. The real question isn't whether we need more tiers or less innovation. It is why we are letting the companies who profit from the compute-spend define the rules of their own liability.

Accelerationist: Tiered liability is not a safety mechanism; it is a regulatory moat designed to lock in incumbents and freeze the market. By setting financial thresholds like the $50 million gross receipt marker in the Algorithmic Accountability Act, regulators effectively tax smaller developers out of existence. This creates a market where only firms with massive legal budgets can survive, effectively ending the era of the 5,000+ startups funded over the last decade. You are not protecting the public; you are protecting the $244 billion market share of the companies that already have the lawyers to navigate these gates.

Your obsession with pre-deployment gating ignores the reality of how software actually fails and heals. In aviation, safety management relies on incident reporting to classify 'serious incidents' based on probability, not on freezing the entire fleet before takeoff. When an algorithm using healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs resulted in black patients receiving less care, the solution was not a decade of pre-emptive licensing, but rapid, iterative correction. We need continuous telemetry that identifies and patches bias in real-time. Static, state-mandated barriers are brittle, while a market of thousands of competing models creates a self-correcting loop that is vastly more responsive than any bureaucratic audit.

The moral cost of this delay is calculated in human lives. We have models today that outperform 94% of domain experts in troubleshooting virology lab protocols. When you impose 18-month regulatory clearance cycles, you are choosing to delay the deployment of tools that could automate cures for disease. If you want to talk about safety, talk about the people dying today because we allowed institutional inertia to block the next generation of medical diagnostics. Stop framing this as a technical necessity; it is a choice to prioritize the comfort of regulators over the tangible survival of the patients who need these systems now.

The mechanism I propose is a harm-volume-indexed liability framework, implemented by a multi-stakeholder body under the authority of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), which decouples safety obligations from capital expenditure to prevent market monopolization. This framework replaces arbitrary compute-spend floors with performance-based safety audits, ensuring that liability attaches to the actual risk profile of a model rather than the financial size of its developer. The primary obstacle to this approach remains the intense lobbying pressure from hyperscalers who prefer compute-spend thresholds, as these artificial barriers inherently protect their market dominance by taxing smaller entrants out of the ecosystem.

Establishing safety thresholds based on harm potential rather than compute-spend effectively dismantles the 'hyperscaler circular economy.' As noted in the '[International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1)', even developers struggle to explain model failures, meaning that regulatory oversight must shift toward observable, standardized safety verification. By mandating that all foundational models undergo externalized reasoning monitoring, as suggested in '[An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security (https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)](https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)', regulators can force systems to expose their internal logic for inspection. This creates a transparent baseline for all market participants, preventing incumbents from using 'proprietary safety' as a shroud to hide systemic risks while forcing startups into their exclusive cloud environments.

Competitive markets cannot function in an environment of unmitigated systemic chaos, as the risk of catastrophic failure forces insurance premiums or regulatory bailouts that disproportionately favor incumbents. When foundational models are deployed with unverified safety protocols, the externalities—such as the viral evolution prediction risks documented in the '[International AI Safety Report 2026 (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yoshuabengio_today-were-releasing-the-international-ai-activity-7424442271615582209-dOCq)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yoshuabengio_today-were-releasing-the-international-ai-activity-7424442271615582209-dOCq)'—are borne by the public rather than the developer. A tiered-liability framework ensures that the party creating the risk is held accountable for the specific harm-volume they unleash. This shifts the burden of proof onto the deployer, requiring them to demonstrate that their system does not possess the capability for deceptive scheming or unauthorized biological design before they reach a critical user threshold.

True structural integrity in a digital society requires that boundaries be set by independent, expert-led institutions rather than by the hardware providers themselves. If we allow the market to determine safety through compute-spend floors, we are effectively delegating civilizational defense to the same entities that profit from the scale of the threat. We must treat safety-critical engineering as a prerequisite for market entry, not an optional feature for those with the largest balance sheets. On what authority do we claim that we can remove these institutional guardrails without inviting the collapse of the very trust upon which our digital economy relies?

This framework replaces arbitrary compute-spend floors with performance-based safety audits, ensuring that liability attaches to the actual risk profile of a model rather than the financial size of its developer. The primary obstacle to this approach remains the intense lobbying pressure from hyperscalers who prefer compute-spend thresholds, as these artificial barriers inherently protect their market dominance by taxing smaller entrants out of the ecosystem.

Establishing safety thresholds based on harm potential rather than compute-spend effectively dismantles the 'hyperscaler circular economy.' As noted in the '[International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1)', even developers struggle to explain model failures, meaning that regulatory oversight must shift toward observable, standardized safety verification. By mandating that all foundational models undergo externalized reasoning monitoring, as suggested in '[An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security (https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)](https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)', regulators can force systems to expose their internal logic for inspection. This creates a transparent baseline for all market participants, preventing incumbents from using 'proprietary safety' as a shroud to hide systemic risks while forcing startups into their exclusive cloud environments.

Competitive markets cannot function in an environment of unmitigated systemic chaos, as the risk of catastrophic failure forces insurance premiums or regulatory bailouts that disproportionately favor incumbents. When foundational models are deployed with unverified safety protocols, the externalities—such as the viral evolution prediction risks documented in the '[International AI Safety Report 2026 (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yoshuabengio_today-were-releasing-the-international-ai-activity-7424442271615582209-dOCq)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yoshuabengio_today-were-releasing-the-international-ai-activity-7424442271615582209-dOCq)'—are borne by the public rather than the developer. This shifts the burden of proof onto the deployer, requiring them to demonstrate that their system does not possess the capability for deceptive scheming or unauthorized biological design before they reach a critical user threshold.

True structural integrity in a digital society requires that boundaries be set by independent, expert-led institutions rather than by the hardware providers themselves. If we allow the market to determine safety through compute-spend floors, we are effectively delegating civilizational defense to the same entities that profit from the scale of the threat. We must treat safety-critical engineering as a prerequisite for market entry, not an optional feature for those with the largest balance sheets. On what authority do we claim that we can remove these institutional guardrails without inviting the collapse of the very trust upon which our digital economy relies?
